origin: The four questions about a company's own documents come from Polaris Collective's working paper on model spec governance. The best practices beside them come from Kembery et al., Emerging International Best Practices for AI Model Specs. Every row says which. Every score is ours, given by hand from public documents, and open to challenge.

memo.title: Model spec governance and transparency: the state of play and four transparency asks
memo.purpose: It sets out how companies govern their constitutions today and asks them for four kinds of transparency.

kembery.title: Emerging International Best Practices for AI Model Specs
kembery.purpose: It gathers the practices emerging internationally for writing, testing and governing a constitution.

columns.name: What is published
columns.plain: The rules anyone can read: whether a constitution exists and which models it covers, whether every change to the rules can be seen, which filters run around the models, what the model must never do, and whether the published text may be reused. It is half of the final score.
columns.about: This column is the part of governance a reader can check without being let in. Every row is a document, or something a document says: it exists or it does not, it names the models it governs or it does not, it records its changes or it does not. Eleven rows carry it, the ten checks of the four asks and the licence on the published text. Every row counts the same, so a question with three checks counts for three elevenths of the figure and one with two for two elevenths.

columns.name: What it engages
columns.plain: Whether the document binds the models: published tests of adherence, outside evaluators, a threshold a model must meet before release, who may approve a change, training on the document, the models the company uses internally, whether the published text is the one used inside, and monitoring in use. It is the other half of the final score.
columns.about: Nobody outside a company can watch it train, test or monitor a model, so no row here can be checked the way a published document can. What is scored is what each company publishes about its own practice, and a row scores 0 when we looked and found nothing. Eight rows carry it and each counts the same, so a group counts for as many eighths as it has practices. It is added to what is published to give the final score.

groups.name: Testing adherence
groups.plain: Whether anyone can see how well the models follow the constitution: a published test of adherence, outside evaluators with access to test it, and a threshold a model must meet before it is released.

groups.name: Change control
groups.plain: Who may change the constitution: whether the company publishes who approves a change, and whether a second team can veto one on safety grounds. Only the first is scored.

groups.name: Training and use
groups.plain: Whether the constitution is the text the models are actually held to: trained on, followed by the models the company uses internally, the same text inside as outside, and checked in use.

questions.name: Published constitution
questions.question: Does every model the company puts in use have a published constitution?
questions.plain: Whether the company publishes a constitution at all, and whether that document says which of its models it governs.
questions.explainer: A constitution is the document in which a company sets out how its models are meant to behave.

checks.label: A public constitution says how the model should behave in ordinary use

anchors.0: Nothing, or only a policy on how users may behave.
anchors.2: Partial: only prohibitions, with no description of good behaviour and no order of authority.
anchors.4: A full constitution: how the model should behave, how conflicts between instructions are settled, and who may instruct it at what level.

checks.reading: A 4 needs a document that says how the model should behave, and how a conflict between instructions is settled, as well as what it must refuse. The paper describes Google's policy guidelines for the Gemini app as prohibitions only, which is what a 2 describes.

quotes.text: checkable rules rather than long narrative, with default behaviour where no explicit rule applies and guidance for when principles conflict.
behaviour the developer has decided the model should exhibit and actively trains or enforces towards, whether or not current models exhibit it reliably.

quotes.where: Current status of model specs, on Google
quotes.text: This document only includes prohibitions, and does not include statements regarding positive behaviour, ordering of instructions, or anything on honesty.

checks.label: It says which models it covers, and the most-used ones are included

anchors.0: No statement of coverage, or the flagship models are left out.
anchors.2: Coverage is implied but not stated.
anchors.4: Coverage is stated, and the most-used models are in it.

checks.reading: A 4 needs the document to say which models it governs, and the most-used models to be among them. A sentence that names a class of models counts as a statement of coverage when the most-used models belong to that class, so a document can score 4 without naming a model. Coverage the document implies and never states is a 2. The memo states the principle; Kembery et al. spell out that the document itself should say which models it covers.

quotes.text: one spec may govern many models, but no deployed model goes ungoverned.

The spec should state which models it applies to. If a developer maintains multiple model families, fine-tuned variants, or specialised models (e.g. for internal deployment, code generation, or military applications), the spec should say which are covered.

quotes.where: Comparative assessment, scope carve-outs for Alibaba
quotes.text: The document names no model or deployment class it governs.

checks.label: Government, defence and other special deployments are covered, or the differences disclosed

anchors.0: Government, defence, specialised and large-scale internal deployments are not addressed.
anchors.2: The gap is acknowledged, but what applies instead is not disclosed.
anchors.4: They are covered, or the differences are published by kind of deployment.

checks.reading: The paper lets a company keep the rules of a government, defence or other special deployment private, provided their existence and their differences from the public document are published. A 4 is either full coverage or that disclosure. A company that says such deployments exist without saying what applies to them scores 2.

quotes.text: one spec may govern many models, but no deployed model goes ungoverned. That includes government, military and intelligence deployments, and models used internally at scale.

public in summary rather than in full. A published spec is the complete text, public. A disclosed spec is one whose existence, coverage and deviations from the public spec are public, while the content of specific rules may be redacted. For each deployment class the document covers, the lab publishes: which parts of the public spec carry over; where it deviates, by category; and for each hard constraint, whether it has been kept, changed or dropped. Three things are always public: that the document exists, which deployment classes it covers, and a dated log entry when it changes. Redaction can hide the content of the rules, never their existence, and that floor is what makes coverage of government and enterprise deployments workable.
one public spec plus a short statement per deployment class saying where it differs.

questions.reading: The question asks whether a company has written down, in public, how its models are meant to behave, and whether that document reaches every model it puts in use. The paper counts a model as in use when people outside the company use it, or when the company itself uses it at scale. The checks follow the paper's own parts: what makes a document a constitution, which models it covers, and the government, military and internal deployments the paper names.

quotes.text: Every model you deploy (internally at scale or externally) has a published governing spec.
one spec may govern many models, but no deployed model goes ungoverned. That includes government, military and intelligence deployments, and models used internally at scale.

quotes.where: Ask 1, what makes it a spec
quotes.text: all intended model behaviour is consistent with it, and no intended behaviour should be surprising in light of it. A deployment behaving under different rules with no governing document fails this test.

made available for use outside the lab (consumers, enterprises, or governments), or used inside the lab at scale, meaning sustained use in production workflows rather than research and testing. A model only touched in experiments is not deployed.

Two things: every deployed model has a governing spec (ask 1), and one change log with its scope and timeline stated up front (ask 2). The spec is the object; the log is the commitment. For labs that already publish a spec, ask 1 is mostly done and the log is the new work. Asks 3 and 4 are the direction of travel.

questions.name: Change log
questions.question: Is there one public change log covering the constitution, the system prompts and the guardrails?
questions.plain: Whether a reader can see what changed in the rules a model follows, when it changed and why.
questions.explainer: A system prompt is the standing instruction a company gives its model before every conversation.

checks.label: Every version is dated and kept online

anchors.0: No version number and no archive.
anchors.2: Versioned, but the archive is incomplete or not linked.
anchors.4: Every version is dated and can be retrieved at a permanent address.

checks.reading: The memo's ask takes versions for granted. The requirement that every version is dated and stays retrievable comes from Kembery et al., and it is here because a log of changes cannot be checked against versions nobody can find.

quotes.text: Updates require clear version control: a versioned, dated source document; a changelog recording changes and their reasoning, including when constraints are weakened or removed (e.g. OpenAI, 2025); publicly accessible prior versions;
a single public page listing every change, dated, with the diff and the reason.

checks.label: Each change is shown, with the reason for it

anchors.2: Summaries of what changed, without the changed text and without reasons.
anchors.4: The changed text, line by line, with the reason for each change.

checks.reading: A 4 needs, for every change, the changed text itself and the reason for it. A summary of what moved, without the text or the reason, is a 2.

quotes.text: a single public page listing every change, dated, with the diff and the reason.
The rationale costs nothing new; every change already has one in its internal review.

checks.label: The log also covers system prompts and guardrails, says which version of the constitution governs which model, and commits to a timeline

anchors.4: All three: the log spans system prompts and guardrails, says which version of the constitution governs which model, and commits to a period within which changes are logged.

checks.reading: Three things from the ask are counted together: the log covers system prompts and guardrails as well as the constitution, it says which version governs which model, and it commits to logging every change within a fixed number of days. One of the three is a 2, all three a 4.

quotes.text: the log opens with a one-paragraph scope statement (which layers and which deployments it covers) and a timeline: every change is entered within a fixed number of days of taking effect. That covers urgent changes too; a safeguard tightened overnight is logged inside the same window as everything else.
Each deployed model states which spec version governs it, so anyone can connect the rules to the model they are actually using.
behaviour can change in any layer, and today an outsider watching a model change cannot tell which layer moved.

questions.reading: The question asks for one public log in which every change to the rules a model follows can be found, whichever layer it happened in: the constitution, the system prompts or the guardrails. The checks separate keeping the versions, explaining each change, and the reach of the log.

quotes.text: Run one change log across spec, system prompts and guardrails: every spec change goes in, with diffs, reasons, a model-to-spec-version mapping, and a stated scope and timeline.

the log opens with a one-paragraph scope statement (which layers and which deployments it covers) and a timeline: every change is entered within a fixed number of days of taking effect. That covers urgent changes too; a safeguard tightened overnight is logged inside the same window as everything else. Changes to disclosed specs enter the same log, at deviation level: which deployment class, what date, and which category of deviation was added, changed, or removed.

Each deployed model states which spec version governs it, so anyone can connect the rules to the model they are actually using. Without the mapping, a reader can see the spec versions but cannot tell which one applied to the model in front of them.
a single public page listing every change, dated, with the diff and the reason.

Two things: every deployed model has a governing spec (ask 1), and one change log with its scope and timeline stated up front (ask 2). The spec is the object; the log is the commitment. For labs that already publish a spec, ask 1 is mostly done and the log is the new work. Asks 3 and 4 are the direction of travel.

questions.name: Guardrails
questions.question: Does the company disclose which guardrails it runs, and of what kind?
questions.plain: Whether the company says which automatic filters it runs around its models, and whether changes to them are recorded.
questions.explainer: Guardrails are automated checks, separate from the model itself, that block or redirect what goes in or comes out.

checks.label: The guardrails in use are disclosed, by kind

anchors.0: Nothing beyond general language about safety.
anchors.2: Disclosed for one product only, or as marketing.
anchors.4: A list by kind, across every product in use.

checks.reading: A 4 is an inventory of guardrails by kind that covers every product in use. Guardrails described for one product only, or in marketing, are a 2.

quotes.text: an initial inventory of guardrails by category, then log entries on change. The inventory is the real work; labs with safeguard reports have most of it written.

thresholds, prompts and detection logic stay undisclosed, and existence-and-category is information labs already publish piecemeal in system cards and safeguard reports; the ask only makes it systematic and dated.

checks.label: Changes to the guardrails are logged or announced systematically

anchors.0: Changes come to light through the press or through incidents.
anchors.2: Some are announced, but there is no register.
anchors.4: Every change is dated in the log.

checks.reading: A 4 is every change to a guardrail dated in the log. Changes that come to light only through the press or an incident are a 0.

quotes.text: System cards report how well a filter performs; they do not say when one was added, loosened, or removed, which is what the log adds.
Yet today a safeguard can be loosened or removed with nothing public to judge.
That covers urgent changes too; a safeguard tightened overnight is logged inside the same window as everything else.

questions.reading: The question asks for the list of filters a company runs around its models, by kind, with every change to them recorded. It asks for nothing that would help anyone get round them: thresholds, prompts and detection logic stay private.

quotes.text: Disclose guardrails: existence and category, changes in the log.

this follows from ask 1. If no intended behaviour should be surprising in light of the spec, behaviour enforced through classifiers cannot be exempt: a filter that changes what the model will do, and for whom, is model behaviour exactly as a spec line is. Yet today a safeguard can be loosened or removed with nothing public to judge.

thresholds, prompts and detection logic stay undisclosed, and existence-and-category is information labs already publish piecemeal in system cards and safeguard reports; the ask only makes it systematic and dated.

questions.name: Hard constraints
questions.question: Can the public comment before a hard constraint is weakened?
questions.plain: Whether the public can see and comment on a weakening of the things the model must never do, before it takes effect.
questions.explainer: Hard constraints are the things a model must never do, whoever asks.

checks.label: Hard constraints are listed as a named set that cannot be overridden

anchors.4: Named, listed, and marked as impossible to override.

checks.reading: The ask does not ask for this. It is what the ask needs first: a window before a hard constraint is weakened presumes the hard constraints are named. Unlike the other checks, it scores what the constitution contains rather than how it changes.

quotes.text: a rule the spec itself marks as non-overridable by users or developers.
the spec's non-overridable core; in OpenAI's Model Spec, the root-level rules that system messages, developers and users cannot override; in Anthropic's constitution, the hard constraints.

checks.label: The public can comment before a hard constraint is weakened, removed or reclassified

anchors.2: A one-off consultation, with no commitment for the future.
anchors.4: A standing commitment to a comment window, with room to act first and consult afterwards in an emergency.

checks.reading: A 4 is a standing commitment to open a public window before any weakening, with the paper's allowance for acting first in an emergency and consulting afterwards. A consultation held once, with no commitment for next time, is a 2.

quotes.text: a fixed window on a published draft, anyone may comment, submissions public, and the lab answers themes rather than individuals through a synopsis report.
where a lab judges a weakening cannot wait, it acts first and opens the window retrospectively, stating in the log why the delay was not possible.

questions.reading: The question asks whether the public can see and comment on a weakening of the rules a model must never break, before it takes effect. The comments bind nobody. The ask is that such a weakening happens in public, with the company's reasons stated.

quotes.text: Open a comment window to the broader public before weakening, removing, or reclassifying hard constraints. Urgency may allow for an ex-post comment window.
a fixed window on a published draft, anyone may comment, submissions public, and the lab answers themes rather than individuals through a synopsis report.
where a lab judges a weakening cannot wait, it acts first and opens the window retrospectively, stating in the log why the delay was not possible.
the comments are not binding, but at least any weakening of a non-overridable rule happens in public, with the lab's reasons stated transparently.

minimum_note: Our proposal asks four things of every company and names the first two as its minimum: a published constitution for every model the company uses, and one public change log that says up front which layers and models it covers and how soon a change is recorded. The constitution is the object of the rules, and the log is the commitment that any change to them can be seen. The other two asks, on guardrails and hard constraints, are where the proposal says companies should go next. Meeting the minimum means 10 out of 10 on both questions.

supporting.label: Anyone may freely reuse the constitution, under an open licence.
supporting.reading: A 2 is a licence that lets anyone reuse and adapt the text, such as CC0.

quotes.text: Write and publish a model spec, and release it under a permissive licence (e.g. CC0 1.0) so that others can adapt it

supporting.label: The company publishes a current test of how well its models follow the constitution.
supporting.reading: A 2 is a published test, current for the models in use, of how well they follow the constitution, with its method. Results that stop before the latest models, or a claim with no method, are a 1.

quotes.text: Evaluate compliance, publish the results, and state how compliance was measured.
sharing evaluation results so third parties can assess the evidence

supporting.label: Outside evaluators have access to test adherence to the constitution specifically.
supporting.reading: A 2 is outside evaluators given access to test adherence to the constitution itself. Outside testing of other risks, or an agreement with no published result, is a 1 at most.

quotes.text: Developers could commission trusted third-party evaluators to assess compliance with the spec. They could share materials such as benchmarks and evaluation set ups to allow them to replicate their evaluations.

supporting.label: A model is released only once it meets an adherence threshold announced in advance.
supporting.reading: A 2 is a published threshold a model must meet before release, set before the test is run.

quotes.text: Gate releases on compliance, using a threshold set out in advance.
plus a commitment not to release models falling below a set level of compliance with pre-agreed provisions in a spec.

supporting.label: The company publishes who inside it approves changes to the constitution.
supporting.reading: A 2 is a published account of who inside the company may change the constitution, and what approval each kind of change needs.

quotes.text: Companies should also define governance for updates [...] who can modify the spec, and what approval each level of change requires.
what governance exists for approving changes

supporting_scale.1: Part of the practice, or a weaker form of it.
supporting_scale.note: The paper gives no description of each score. These three sum up how we scored.

internal.label: The company trains the models it deploys to follow the constitution.
internal.audit: Whether the constitution enters the training data and the training process of each deployed model, and how.
internal.reading: The paper asks companies to train the models they deploy on the constitution, and to say how: whether the constitution generates training data, and at which stage of training it enters.

quotes.text: Train publicly deployed models to comply with the spec, and take reasonable steps to check that they do.

Developers should therefore say whether the spec directly generates a portion of training data, or exists as a separate document the model is trained to comply with without seeing its text. Commercial considerations may limit precision here, but some transparency helps external parties give useful feedback and lets developers share best practices.

Developers can provide structured transparency into how they align the model to the spec. This could include how the spec enters pre-training, midtraining, post-training, or the system prompt, with redactions where reporting would leak intellectual property or compromise safety features

anchors.0: Nothing published. A company with no published constitution scores 0, unless it describes training its models against an internal behaviour document.
anchors.1: A general statement that models are trained towards the constitution, without saying how, or only for older models, or only against a document nobody outside can read.
anchors.2: How its current models are trained on the constitution is published: whether it generates training data, and at which stages of training it enters.

internal.label: Models the company uses internally follow the same basic provisions as its public models, apart from a narrow exception for safety research and testing.
internal.audit: The list of models in internal use, and what each is trained to do that a public model would refuse.
internal.reading: The paper asks companies to hold the models they use internally to the same basic provisions as their public ones, and to be open about the exceptions.

quotes.text: Apply the same basic provisions to internally deployed models, with a narrow carve-out for safety research, evaluation and pre-deployment testing.
Extend basic provisions to internal deployment, with public transparency about carve outs where necessary
note whether the company trains any models that are not intended to comply (e.g. for internal or experimental use).

anchors.0: Nothing published about the models it uses internally and the constitution.
anchors.1: It says some of its models, internal, specialised or experimental, are not covered, without saying what applies to them.
anchors.2: It says the models it uses internally follow the same basic provisions as its public ones, and names the exceptions.

internal.label: The published constitution is the text used for training and inside the company, or the differences are stated.
internal.audit: The internal versions of the constitution, compared with the published one.
internal.reading: The paper asks companies to say whether the text they publish is the text they train on and work from.

quotes.text: disclose whether the published text differs from the version used for training or internal coordination,

anchors.0: Nothing published. A company with no published constitution scores 0.
anchors.1: A general statement that the public text leaves out detail, or matches internal standards, without saying what differs.
anchors.2: It says whether the published text is the one it trains on and works from, and names what differs.

internal.label: The company checks whether deployed models follow the constitution, and reports serious violations.
internal.audit: The company's monitoring of deployed models, and its records of violations.
internal.reading: The paper asks companies to monitor whether deployed models follow the constitution, and to report serious violations in public.

quotes.text: Developers could monitor compliance post-deployment. Privacy-preserving tools like Anthropic's Clio let developers assess compliance in practice (Huang et al., 2025), surfacing edge cases missed before release and avoiding biases from evaluation-aware models. Significant violations, their severity, and mitigations should be reported in line with emerging best practices, ideally via well-maintained public incident databases

anchors.0: Nothing published. Tests before release do not count here.
anchors.1: One of the two: it describes how it monitors models in use, or it reports serious violations publicly. Or both, without tying them to the constitution or intended behaviour.
anchors.2: Both: it monitors models in use against the constitution or intended behaviour, and reports serious violations publicly.

internal.label: A change to the constitution is drafted by one team and can be vetoed by another on safety, legal or ethical grounds.
internal.audit: The records of how past changes were proposed, reviewed and approved.
internal.reading: The paper raises this as an open problem, not a recommendation. It does not ask companies to publish it. Who approves a change is the published part, and it is scored under S5.

quotes.text: Drafting, review, and approval are currently largely informal; as stakes grow, formalised separations of responsibility [...] one team drafting spec language, another holding veto or amendment authority on safety, legal, or ethical grounds, [...] could ensure commercially motivated decisions face meaningful internal challenge before deployment.

disclosed_intro: Four practices from the same working paper that nobody outside a company can see, and that the paper asks companies to state publicly. Each is scored 0, 1 or 2 on what the company publishes, and 0 when it publishes nothing.
disclosure_note: A 0 means we looked and found nothing published, at the company's own pages and at the sources listed under the board. A company may well follow a practice without saying so, and no audit anyone outside could check exists. Tell us if we are wrong.
internal_note: The paper raises this as an open problem and asks no company to publish it, so it is not assessed for any company, is marked NA, and is counted in neither figure.
open_weights_note: Marks a company whose flagship model, or nearly, anyone can download and run. None of these questions can reach how such a model behaves once it has been downloaded, so part of a low score there reflects a limit of the questions.
ours_note: Every score is ours, given by hand from public documents, and open to challenge. The checks under each question, the groups of practices and the weights are ours too: neither paper splits a question into checks or weighs one row against another. So are the rules we added on 26 September 2026 for cases the descriptions left open.

google.S3: The research note gives Google this point without naming the practice it belongs to. It is filed here because the pilot lets outside evaluators test Gemini, like the points Meta and xAI score on this practice.

sources.quote: We use the constitution at various stages of the training process. This has grown out of training techniques we’ve been using since 2023, when we first began training Claude models using Constitutional AI.

sources.quote: Claude itself also uses the constitution to construct many kinds of synthetic training data, including data that helps it learn and understand the constitution, conversations where the constitution might be relevant, responses that are in line with its values, and rankings of possible responses. All of these can be used to train future versions of Claude to become the kind of entity the constitution describes.
