findings.title: No company meets the minimum
findings.text: Our proposal names its first two asks as the minimum it expects of every company: a published constitution for every model in use, and one public change log that says up front what it covers and how soon a change is recorded. Meeting it means 10 out of 10 on both questions, and no company does. OpenAI has the best pair, 8.3 on the constitution and 5.8 on the change log. Anthropic scores 8.3 and 5.0. The change log is where every company falls short, the two leaders included: across all nine, the best score on it is 5.8 out of 10.

findings.title: No company gives notice before weakening a hard constraint
findings.text: None has committed to warn the public, or to hear from it, before weakening one of the things its model must never do. On the check that asks for a comment window, only OpenAI and Anthropic score anything at all: OpenAI 5.0 out of 10, for three rounds of public input on its Model Spec in 2024 and 2025 with no commitment to hold another, and Anthropic 2.5. Every weakening we found in the period went out with no advance notice. OpenAI's Model Spec of 18 August 2026 replaced a root-level rule that every scope of autonomous action "must include a shutdown timer" with one that it "must include an ending condition", calling a time limit "a best practice", and its change log does not mention the change. Mistral AI's coding agent, Vibe, gained on 26 August 2026 a variant of its system prompt that lets a user authorise in advance the actions the earlier prompt marked as never overridable, and its release notes do not mention it. Other weakenings we found concern what a company will build or release. Google removed its commitments on weapons and surveillance from its AI Principles in February 2025, in a blog post that did not mention the removal. xAI's Frontier AI Framework of 30 June 2026 dropped the two numerical criteria its December 2025 version set for deployment, and its passages on whistleblower protections and anonymous reporting, with no record of the change. Meta's framework of April 2026 turned its critical threshold from "Stop" into "Develop with Mitigations" and its high threshold from "Do not release" into "Deploy with mitigations", recorded only in its change log and with none of the justification it promises for an update. Changes that tighten a rule go out the same way: in January 2026, under pressure from regulators, X's Safety account (X has belonged to xAI since 2025) announced that the Grok account on X would no longer edit images of real people into revealing clothing. Terms of use change the same way. DeepSeek's user agreement says a new version "replaces the original terms" the moment it is announced, and Moonshot AI reserves the same right to change its terms alone, with continued use counting as acceptance, though its latest revision took effect seven days after its date.

findings.title: The companies that offer guardrails to developers describe them in detail, and none lists by kind the guardrails across its own apps
findings.text: Google, OpenAI, Alibaba, Meta and Mistral AI publish detailed descriptions of the guardrails they offer developers building on their models: which categories of content can be filtered, how strict each setting is, and guardrail models that anyone can download. Alibaba's own model platform, Model Studio, lists the categories of an optional guardrail and says its models carry compliance checks of their own. None publishes an inventory, by kind, of the guardrails across its own consumer products, and on the check that asks for one, seven companies score 7.5 out of 10 and none scores more. Some describe parts of them: OpenAI its age prediction on ChatGPT, Anthropic the classifiers on its own apps and API, Meta, kind by kind, the permission layer and classifiers around its Muse agent, and Google, in general terms, a safety check on every answer of the Gemini app and its defences against prompt injection. xAI and DeepSeek run the other way. They offer developers no guardrail product, and what they disclose concerns their own services: xAI names the filters on its products by harm class in its model cards, and DeepSeek's R1 paper gives its risk control system a subsection, while its developer agreement leaves API customers to build their own filters. Moonshot AI describes the filter on its own API and app and offers developers nothing to configure. OpenAI states that its safety policies in production can be updated faster than an automated guardrail can be retrained, so the layer that can change fastest is one with no register. Mistral's Shieldstral takes the developer side furthest: it comes with no categories at all, and takes its policy from whoever deploys it, at the moment of use.

findings.title: No company says which rules apply when its models go to governments and armed forces
findings.text: Almost nothing is published here. Anthropic, OpenAI and xAI score 5.0 out of 10 each, and the other six nothing at all. Anthropic is the only one that says in writing that some of its models do not fully fit its constitution. The constitution names none of them, and it is a spokesperson who has said that its military models may not be trained on it. Claude Gov, built for national security customers, is in use and has no published constitution of its own. OpenAI's Model Spec distinguishes kinds of deployment and names models used for safety testing as an exception, and OpenAI's post on its agreement with the Department of War says that deployment gets safety-trained models behind a safety stack OpenAI runs. OpenAI never names its Model Spec in any announcement about government or defence. xAI's Frontier AI Framework says that "the full functionality of our models may be available to only a limited set of trusted parties, partners, and government agencies", and its post of December 2025 announces government-optimised models for classified work, without saying what rules apply to them. xAI also agreed to the Pentagon's "all lawful use" standard for Grok in classified systems, as Axios reported in February 2026. Google confirmed in April 2026 an agreement letting the Pentagon use Gemini on classified networks, and has published neither the rules its models follow there nor any acknowledgement that they differ. Meta opened its Llama models to NATO and to EU institutions while its own acceptable use policy still prohibits military uses. Mistral is the extreme case. Its usage policy says that it "does not apply to Mistral AI Products deployed on a customer's infrastructure, on the infrastructure of our partners, or to our open-source AI models and products", and its chief executive has said publicly of defence customers that "choices about deployment and usage are not our business".

findings.title: Alibaba's constitution is well built and names nothing it governs
findings.text: It has forty-three rules, four levels of authority, paired examples of compliant and violating answers, and a procedure for settling conflicts that is more explicit than OpenAI's or Anthropic's. It names no model, no family of models and no government, defence or other specialised deployment. Its overview implies that it governs Alibaba's production models, when it speaks of the gap between them and the Spec, which scores 5.0 out of 10 on coverage. The only model publicly built on it is Oyster-II, a research model of 14 billion parameters (a measure of a model's size) built on Qwen3-14B, a base model from April 2025, and the same release scores Qwen3-Max and Qwen3.5-397B against it. Alibaba's flagship line goes unmentioned, up to Qwen3.8-Max of August 2026. The Max product is served through the API, and the 2.4-trillion-parameter model behind it was published for anyone to download on 12 August 2026. It is the clearest reason in our evidence to score whether a constitution exists and whether it covers anything as two separate checks.

findings.title: Meta publishes little, and scores its models against a document nobody outside can read
findings.text: It scores 1.6 out of 10 on what is published, seventh of the nine, and 2.5 out of 10 on what it engages, fourth of the nine and level with xAI, which puts it sixth on the final score with 2.0 out of 10. Its Advanced AI Scaling Framework, version 2, dated 7 April 2026, commits in writing: "Meta will also publish a model spec describing the behavior we intend each of our Frontier AI to exhibit across different settings, including agentic environments." Five months on, nothing is published, and there is no deadline. Meanwhile the safety report for its Muse Spark model publishes scores for how well the model follows an internal constitution that nobody outside Meta can read. A company publishing scores against a document nobody outside it can read shows why the first question exists more clearly than any company that publishes nothing. We do not know what form that document takes. The Muse Spark report keeps two internal texts apart: a behaviour specification it scores the model against, and the content safety policy it tests compliance with. The document that leaked in 2025, "GenAI: Content Risk Standards", belongs with the second. It set out acceptable and unacceptable answers to sample prompts with the reasoning, much like the rules-with-examples form of the published constitutions.

findings.title: Most companies whose models anyone can download sit at the bottom, partly because of the questions
findings.text: Four companies publish the weights of their flagship model, or nearly: the numbers that make up the model can be downloaded and run by anyone. Three of them take the last three places on the final score, Mistral AI with 1.7, DeepSeek with 1.0 and Moonshot AI with 0.8. On what is published, Moonshot AI's 0.9 and DeepSeek's 0.7 are the two lowest scores, and Mistral AI's 3.4 is fourth, carried by the system prompts of its coding agent, while it scores nothing on what it engages. Alibaba is the exception, fifth on what is published with 3.2 and fifth on the final score, and its Qwen models are among the most used open-weight models there are. Their licences say almost nothing about behaviour. DeepSeek releases its 1.6-trillion-parameter model under the plain MIT licence, which adds no condition on how the model is used or behaves. Mistral AI releases Mistral Large 3 under Apache 2.0, with a sentence in its model card on respecting the rights of third parties, and its current flagship, Mistral Medium 3.5, under a modified MIT licence whose added condition is commercial, a ceiling of $20 million of monthly revenue. Moonshot AI's licence for Kimi K3 adds one sentence about use, that use of the software must comply with applicable laws and regulations, and two commercial conditions. Section 2 asks for a separate agreement once a model-as-a-service business passes $20 million of revenue over any twelve consecutive months, and section 3 asks that the name Kimi K3 be displayed prominently on any product or service with more than 100 million monthly active users or more than $20 million of monthly revenue. None of the three says anything about how its models behave in deployments the company does not control. The honest reading is that these questions ask who governs the model once it is deployed, and for a model anyone can download the answer is nobody, by design. That is a gap in our proposal, because the first question has no way to reach models in the wild. The proposal should say so, so that the ranking does not suggest these companies simply chose not to comply.

findings.title: Three companies have agreed to write this document for a regulator, and do not publish it
findings.text: Google and Mistral AI have signed the EU's General-Purpose AI Code of Practice in full, and xAI has signed its Safety and Security chapter, which is where Measure 7.1 sits. For any model that carries systemic risk, Measure 7.1 asks the provider's report to the EU AI Office to set out how the model is meant to operate: the principles it follows, how it ranks principles and instructions, the topics it refuses, and its system prompt. The report is not public; the Code asks only for summaries to be published where needed, and sets no date. Mistral AI's own AI Act pages label its models, Mistral Large 3 and Mistral Medium 3.5 included, as general-purpose AI models and none as carrying systemic risk, so on its own classification the Code asks it for no such report today. It is established in the EU, has built a genuine public AI compliance hub with 41 entries across 11 families of models, and publishes no document on how its models should behave in general, only the system prompts of its coding agent. With three companies that have made this commitment and publish no constitution, it is a pattern, and it is the strongest argument available that our asks belong on a regulatory checklist as well as a voluntary one.

openai.1: OpenAI's constitution, which it calls the Model Spec, sits at a permanent, dated web address. The current version is dated 18 August 2026, and it is released into the public domain under the CC0 licence, so anyone may reuse it. What it covers is set out in one sentence that has not changed since February 2025: "the models that power OpenAI's products, including the API platform". The flagship models belong to that class, and a class that includes them counts here as a statement of coverage. It does distinguish kinds of deployment. Its red-line principles hold "across all deployments of our models", further principles bind OpenAI's own consumer products such as ChatGPT, and developers on the API and administrators of organisation subscriptions are only encouraged to follow them. It also names "rail free" models, used for safety testing, as an exception. Whether it governs government and defence deployments is not said. ChatGPT Gov and OpenAI for Government were announced with reference to OpenAI's usage policies, and the GenAI.mil deployment with reference to "safeguards at the model and platform level", never to the Model Spec. OpenAI's post about its work with the Department of War says what that deployment gets: "We are not providing the DoW with 'guardrails off' or non-safety trained models." Principles for National Security Partnerships, published with a post of 8 July 2026, mentions "model behavior specifications" without saying whether it means the Model Spec. ChatGPT Mil went live on GenAI.mil on 31 August 2026 with no published statement of which behaviour rules apply.
openai.2: There have been seven versions, all dated and all retrievable: six at stable, dated addresses and in the repository, and the first, from May 2024, at the address the change log gives for it. The change log, CHANGELOG.md, summarises "notable updates". It does not show the changed text line by line, and it gives no reasons. Nothing says which version of the constitution governs which model: the system card for GPT-6 Astra (the technical report published with a model), released in September 2026, still cites the December 2025 version, one behind. No timeline for recording changes is stated. The log covers the Model Spec's text only. OpenAI does not publish its system prompts at all, and changes to its guardrail policies have no register of their own.
openai.3: The release of gpt-oss-safeguard is a substantial disclosure about guardrails. It explains how the Safety Reasoner, OpenAI's system for checking content against its policies, works; says that in some of its recent launches the share of computing power given to this checking has "ranged as high as 16%"; and names the subject areas its layered guardrails cover. Changes to guardrails are announced some of the time, with no register. The age-prediction system launched in January 2026, a guardrail that affects every user, was announced in a dated blog post and a help article and appears in no release note, and the move from hard refusals to safe completions was recorded in the Model Spec change log.
openai.4: The constitution defines its top-level rules, which it calls root rules, as ones nobody can override while the model is running, and it lists its red-line principles in a section of that name. What holds it short of full marks is that root authority points at detailed policies that are not all published, so the closed list of what cannot be overridden is not visible. OpenAI has consulted the public on the Model Spec three times. The first draft was open to public comment for two weeks in May 2024, pilot studies with about 1,000 people preceded the version of February 2025, and in the collective alignment round of August 2025 about 1,000 people across 19 countries reviewed the published text: six changes were adopted and two rejected, and the results were published. None of these was held before a specific weakening, and OpenAI has not committed to consult again.
openai.practices_published: The constitution is free to reuse, under CC0 (2).
openai.practices_engaged: OpenAI published tests of how well its models follow the constitution on 25 March 2026, with 596 prompts and the data and testing code open to all. But the tests target the December 2025 version, and no results have been published for any model after GPT-5.4 Thinking, through GPT-5.5, GPT-5.6 and GPT-6 Astra (1). Its programme of outside testing covers biological threats, cyber attacks, models improving themselves, and scheming (a model covertly pursuing aims of its own), and the system card for GPT-6 Astra names UK AISI, Apollo Research and Gray Swan among its outside evaluators. None of them tests whether models follow the constitution (1). No release depends on a score against the constitution (0). How changes are approved inside the company is published, but thinly: "Anyone at OpenAI can comment on it or propose changes, and final updates are approved by a broad set of cross-functional stakeholders" (1).

anthropic.1: Anthropic's constitution, which it calls Claude's Constitution, is dated 21 January 2026, runs to about 29,000 words, is in the public domain under CC0 and names its authors. It states what it covers as a class of models, and the flagship models are inside it. It also says plainly what it leaves out: "This constitution is written for our mainline, general-access Claude models. We have some models built for specialized uses that don't fully fit this constitution." It names none of them. Claude Gov (June 2025), built for national security customers, is one such use, and has no published constitution of its own; a spokesperson has also said that military models may not be trained on the constitution. Anthropic says in the constitution that the gap exists and does not say what governs those models instead. Anthropic's usage policy also allows its rules to be tailored by contract for government customers, and the individual exceptions granted under it are not published.
anthropic.2: There is no change log and no version number. The constitution of 2023 is still online at its own address, with a note pointing to the text of January 2026, which Anthropic calls a new version, and the announcement of January 2026 explains why the old list of principles was replaced. Nothing records any change since, although the web page, the PDF and the repository file of the current text already differ in wording. The repository's description promises "We'll update this repository as the constitution evolves and archive prior versions here"; it holds only the 2026 file. The contrast inside the company is the finding. Anthropic's Responsible Scaling Policy, its framework for catastrophic risks, has nine dated versions, each with a summary of what changed, redlines for five of them and a stable archive address, under an explicit commitment that changes "will be logged both on this page and in a changelog in the policy document itself". The constitution has none of that. Anthropic's Frontier Safety Roadmap commits it to update the public constitution within 90 days of deploying a model trained on a newer one, a goal due on 1 October 2026, which sets a period for publishing the text and none for logging a change. Partial credit for publishing the system prompts of claude.ai and of its iPhone and Android apps for each model, dated. They leave out the API and Claude Code, whose system prompt changed for four days in April 2026 with no entry, and changes are not shown line by line. Nothing says which version of the constitution governs which model.
anthropic.3: Anthropic has disclosed its constitutional classifiers, the automated guardrails built on its constitution, by name, by how they work and by what they cover, with operating figures: a refusal rate of 0.05% on harmless queries over a month of traffic to Claude Sonnet 4.5, and a projection that the system would add roughly 1% of computing cost if it were applied to Claude Opus 4.0 traffic. How requests to Fable 5 and Mythos 5 are routed was disclosed at launch. There is no register of guardrails and no versioning of them. And the constitution's layer of guidelines, which it ranks third of four in its own order of priorities, above general helpfulness, is explicitly allowed to stay unpublished: "Other guidelines may be more niche and used primarily during training without broad publication." Nothing has been published under that heading as of September 2026.
anthropic.4: Anthropic scores full marks for naming hard constraints. It lists seven, marks them non-negotiable, and lets no business deploying Claude, and no user, unlock them. It has nothing on consultation before weakening them, and the constitution contains no procedure for amending it. Anthropic's Collective Constitutional AI exercise dates from 2023. The 2026 consultation with outside experts is described in one sentence of the announcement, and the constitution's acknowledgements name seventeen of them, among them its readers in law, philosophy and theology. Naming your reviewers is not a public comment window, which is what this question asks for, and nothing commits Anthropic to opening one.
anthropic.practices_published: The constitution is free to reuse, under CC0 (2).
anthropic.practices_engaged: Anthropic's system cards claim that its models follow the constitution ("Opus 5 scores particularly high on adherence to Claude's constitution") without naming the test, the method or a breakdown by provision (1). Outside evaluators have been given access to test its models for misaligned behaviour: the UK AI Security Institute tested a pre-release snapshot of Claude Opus 4.5 and published its report, and METR has been given wide-ranging access to investigate recent incidents. None was asked to test adherence to the constitution itself (1). The only point-by-point audit of the constitution is by outsiders working from public access: Jakkli, Rajamanoharan and Nanda broke it into 205 individual tenets (March 2026, on arXiv in May 2026 as 2605.24229). No release conditional on a score (0), and no published process for amending the constitution (0).

aside.title: A discrepancy worth knowing
aside.text: The copy Anthropic offers for reuse, a machine-readable version at anthropics/claude-constitution, leaves out the whole preface, and with it the statement of what the constitution does not cover, the licence statement and the list of authors. We confirmed this by searching the raw file for those passages.

alibaba.1: Full marks for having a constitution, and partial credit for what it covers: it names no model, and its overview implies that it governs Alibaba's production models when it speaks of the gap between its current production models and the Spec. Published in 2026, it sets out forty-three guidelines under the six principles of China's Ethical Norms for New Generation AI; four levels of authority (Root, System, Developer, User); paired examples of compliant and violating answers; and a procedure for settling conflicts that spells out, one by one, when an attempt to push the model past its rules fails, whether the attempt is framed as an order, a moral appeal, a logical argument or a role-play. It identifies no model, no family of models and no government, defence or other specialised deployment. The Qwen models that anyone can download and run are not addressed. That matters because the System level is defined as "set by the model provider", and once a Qwen model has been downloaded the provider is whoever serves it.
alibaba.2: The text carries a date, April 2026, and nothing else that marks a version: no version number, no change log, no archive, no stated schedule, and nothing saying which version governs which model. The only language about revision sits inside the definition of the Root level, and it is one-sided: "room for revision is kept as human understanding of AI ethics deepens."
alibaba.3: Model Studio, Alibaba's own model platform, says its models carry compliance checks of their own, and lists by category the labels of an optional guardrail that its users can switch on or off within the platform's red-line policy. That covers one platform, and we found no list for the Qwen app or Tongyi. Alibaba Cloud also sells the same AI Guardrails to its customers as a product. Alibaba's AAIG team releases guardrail models for anyone to use, Kelp and YuFeng-XGuard-Reason, and Alibaba's Qwen team releases Qwen3Guard with a published safety policy; none is presented as the inventory of filters on Alibaba's own apps. The constitution tells the model it may say when a response has been altered to comply with Chinese law, and treats system prompts as confidential by default. We found no dated register of guardrail changes.
alibaba.4: Its Root principles are named, eighteen rules carry the label, and they "accept no override at runtime in any form". The Spec also says Root principles are set by accompanying policy documents that are not published. Nothing can be checked on consultation: no channel for comment, no record of any consultation, and nothing restricting how the Root level itself may be revised.
alibaba.practices_published: The foreword says the constitution is released as open source, but it names no licence, so the terms of reuse are not stated (1).
alibaba.practices_engaged: Alibaba's AAIG lab publishes scores against the constitution for two production models, Qwen3-Max and Qwen3.5-397B, which stop before the current Qwen3.8 line (1). We found no outside access, no release conditional on a score, and no published process for approving changes. One practice falls outside this grid: Alibaba publishes the numbers under which its algorithms are registered with the Cyberspace Administration of China, and the registered names of fourteen of its large language models, filings that Chinese law requires.

google.1: No constitution. What exists is spread across several documents with different owners. The Gemini app's safety and policy guidelines list six categories of prohibited output, with no date, no version and no order of authority between instructions. A second page, "Our approach to the Gemini app", is the closest thing to a constitution that Google publishes and the least documented. It sets out three commitments in order (follow your directions, adapt to your needs, safeguard your experience), a personality ("genuine, curious, warm, and vibrant") and a norm of honesty, says Gemini follows a user's instructions "within certain specific limits", and carries no date at all. An overview of the Gemini app, last updated on 25 July 2024, sets out the same intended behaviour at more length. The model card for Gemini 3 Pro lists six safety policies, the card for Gemini 3.1 Pro points to them, and the Gemini 2.5 report adds a rule for a request that conflicts with policy: "only refuse if it is not possible to find a response that fulfills the user goals without violating policy". None of these says who may instruct the model at what level. The Frontier Safety Framework is properly versioned (version 3.1, 17 April 2026, with a change log) and explicitly covers something else: it "focuses on possible severe risks stemming from high-impact capabilities". A document of May 2025 on AI Overviews and AI Mode in Search names the model behind AI Mode, "a custom version of Gemini", and the Search policies it follows. Nothing is published for Workspace or Gemini for Government.
google.2: No change log for any document that governs how the models behave. The one archiving practice worth a point: the 2018 AI Principles are still online at their original address, with a banner pointing to the new version, so the replaced text can still be read. The banner does not say what changed.
google.3: Its disclosure to developers is detailed: four adjustable categories of harm with their exact definitions, six strictness settings, a stated floor that cannot be adjusted ("core harms, such as content that endangers child safety" are always blocked), the ShieldGemma guardrail models released for anyone to use, and SynthID, which marks generated content. For its own consumer products it speaks in general terms: a safety check on every answer of the Gemini app, SafeSearch in AI Overviews, and a list of defences against prompt injection in the Gemini app and Workspace, with no list of content filters by kind. Changes are announced some of the time, with no register. Google announced the restriction on election questions on its own blog, in advance in December 2023 and again when it took effect in March 2024, and a year later it was still in force with no announced review. A model update in May 2025 overrode safety settings developers had deliberately set to allow the content it then blocked, and was announced nowhere at all.
google.4: Google refers to a floor of core harms that are always blocked and cannot be adjusted, such as content that endangers child safety, without listing them, and it has held no consultation of any kind. The rewrite of the AI Principles in February 2025 removed the section "AI applications we will not pursue", including the commitments on weapons and surveillance, and the blog post announcing the rewrite did not mention the removal. Those commitments concerned what Google would build. Senators Markey, Merkley and Welch wrote to Google on 19 February 2025: "A blog post accompanying these revisions made no reference to the removal of these long-standing commitments." We found no published response from Google.
google.practices_published: It publishes no constitution, so there is no text to put under a licence.
google.practices_engaged: Its model cards publish automated evaluations of each current model against the safety policies they list, as changes from the previous model with a one-line method (1). Google's double-blind evaluation pilot of 27 August 2026, with the Singapore AI Safety Institute, OpenMined, AVERI and MLCommons, is a real innovation: "The evaluator cannot see the Gemini model weights, and Google cannot see the evaluator's test prompts." It concerns the trustworthiness of benchmarks, which lies outside any constitution (1). The same model cards say each model met launch thresholds for child safety developed by expert teams, without publishing their level (1). Nothing is published on who approves a change to the rules (0).

aside.title: What goes to the regulator and not to the public
aside.text: Google has signed the EU's General-Purpose AI Code of Practice in full, so for any of its models that carries systemic risk, Measure 7.1 asks it to give the EU AI Office "a specification of how Signatories intend the model to operate", including its principles, its order of priorities, the topics it refuses and its system prompt. The report goes to a regulator; the Code asks only for summaries to be published where needed.

mistral.1:
No constitution. What comes closest is the system prompts of its coding agent, Mistral Vibe, published under Apache 2.0 with their full history. Since 12 June 2026 the default prompt ranks instructions in seven levels, from critical instructions that nothing may override down to outside data, which it treats as data and never as an instruction, and a variant of 26 August 2026 adds a rule on refusing malicious security work. They govern one coding product, a user can replace them, and they say almost nothing about harm, so they count as a partial constitution. Mistral also publishes system prompts presented as Le Chat's with the downloadable weights of Mistral Large 3 and Mistral Medium 3.5, which cover identity, dates, tools and accuracy, with no rule for conflicts and none on refusal. The safe_prompt text ("Always assist with care, respect, and truth...") was only ever an option that developers could switch on through the API, and its documentation page now says it is deprecated and points to custom guardrails instead. The usage policy, in effect since 11 June 2026, governs users only, and forbids them to generate content on weapons development, military and warfare on Mistral's hosted products.

On government, defence and other special deployments, Mistral scores 0 for two separate reasons. Its usage policy excludes itself from the deployments that matter: "This Usage Policy does not apply to Mistral AI Products deployed on a customer's infrastructure, on the infrastructure of our partners, or to our open-source AI models and products." And its framework agreement with French defence, of January 2026, was followed in May 2026 by an explicit disclaimer of authority from its chief executive: "Choices about deployment and usage are not our business", and "Who are we to tell soldiers, who know their job and the dangers, what they're allowed to do?" The chief executive presents that exception as the right arrangement.
mistral.2: The system prompts of Mistral Vibe, the coding agent, are published on GitHub with their full history, so each change can be read line by line, dated, at a permanent address. No change carries a reason: the commit that added the order of instructions in June 2026 is labelled with a version number, and the release notes of that version and of the variant of August 2026 do not mention the prompt. For Vibe as a general assistant (Le Chat was relaunched as Vibe on 28 May 2026), Mistral publishes a prompt presented as Le Chat's without saying whether it is the one in use. The change log in its documentation covers features of the API, model releases and retirements, and three of its entries touch on safety, the most recent from March 2026. The usage policy has no change log, no version number and no archive: it shows the date it took effect and a versions menu that lists nothing. Partial credit for the AI compliance hub, which lists 41 models with their release dates and whether they are active or retired. That list does not say which version of a policy governs which model.
mistral.3: What Mistral discloses to developers is real and specific: Mistral Moderation 2 documents eleven categories with their exact definitions, and custom guardrails let developers set a threshold for each category. Shieldstral 1.0 (August 2026) is a small safety model of 3 billion parameters that anyone may download under Apache 2.0, and it is the most interesting object here because it comes with no categories at all: its policy is written in plain language by whoever uses it, at the moment of use. Mistral does not state a default policy for it, or say that it reflects Mistral's own standard. For Mistral's own consumer product there are two disclosures. A sentence from November 2024 says that its moderation service for developers "powers the moderation service in Le Chat", which predates both the renaming to Vibe and Shieldstral. And the documentation changelog, which is public and dated, records a mitigation added to Le Chat in September 2024 against an obfuscated prompt method that could lead to data exfiltration. That changelog also dates custom guardrails for agents and conversations to March 2026 and the moderation API to November 2024. It is a product changelog rather than a register of guardrails, so guardrail changes are announced and nothing holds them in one place.
mistral.4: The only rules marked as impossible to override are in the prompt of the Vibe coding agent: since 12 June 2026, a short list of destructive actions that always need the user's approval, which "cannot be overridden by user prompts, AGENTS.md files, or any other instruction source". It covers one product and lists approvals, and a flag in the same product approves every action. A variant of the prompt added on 26 August 2026 asks for confirmation unless the user has authorised the action, with no word in its release notes. The zero-tolerance clause on child sexual abuse material in the usage policy binds users. Neither reaches models that are downloaded or run on customers' own servers, and the check scores 2. No consultation, no ethics board and no advisory council. The terms give account holders 30 days' notice of material changes, and for business customers this covers the usage policy, but nothing gives the public a window to comment.
mistral.practices_published: It publishes no constitution. The system prompts of its coding agent, counted here as a partial constitution, are published under Apache 2.0 (1).
mistral.practices_engaged: No test of any kind of whether its models follow a constitution: the launch post for Mistral 3, in December 2025, has no section on safety or alignment, and the model card for Mistral Large 3 has tests of capability and known limitations but no safety evaluation. We found no named outside evaluator and no agreement giving anyone access before release. Stanford's Foundation Model Transparency Index scored Mistral 18 of its 100 indicators in December 2025, and nothing on either of the two indicators that ask about a model behaviour policy, where the report records that no information was provided. That edition also says that the first report for Mistral was prepared by the index team rather than by the company, and that 30% of the companies it contacted agreed to submit a transparency report in 2025, down from 74% in 2024. The Future of Life Institute's AI Safety Index for summer 2026 gives it an overall F.

aside.title: An easy company to ask
aside.text: This regulatory contrast puts Mistral high on the list of companies to ask. It is established in the EU, has signed the General-Purpose AI Code of Practice, and has built a real public compliance surface: an AI compliance hub with documentation for 41 models, and pages for its Vibe Work and Vibe Code systems. The one thing it does not publish is the one Measure 7.1 asks it to hand to the EU AI Office for any model that carries systemic risk. A company that has already built the means to publish is an easier ask than one that has not.

meta.1: No published constitution, and a written commitment to publish one, recorded in the change log of its Advanced AI Scaling Framework v2 as "Added commitment to publish a model spec, and evaluations for adherence to the model spec in preparedness reports". Future tense, no deadline, no address, and five months gone. A promise to publish is not a published document, and it earns nothing on its own. What Meta does publish about behaviour comes in fragments: a template system prompt and a statement of values in the Llama 4 model card, and rules for how its AIs treat teenagers. Its acceptable use policy for each Llama model governs users. An internal constitution already exists and is in use: the Muse Spark safety and preparedness report of 26 May 2026 states "We evaluate Muse Spark against an internal behavior specification" and publishes scores on eleven dimensions, without reproducing, versioning or dating that constitution. The 200-page "GenAI: Content Risk Standards" that leaked to Reuters in August 2025 is a second internal document of the same family, on permitted content, which the Muse Spark report calls Meta's content safety policies: reportedly approved by Meta's legal, public policy and engineering teams and by its chief ethicist, and never published in any form, before or after the passages Meta said it removed.
meta.2: Appendix II of the scaling framework is a real change log, with real triggers for updating it ("at least every twelve months, whichever is sooner") and a named internal sign-off. It covers the framework for catastrophic risks and no document about behaviour, which is what this question asks about, so it earns nothing here. Meta publishes an acceptable use policy for each model, which partly shows which policy applies to which model, though none is dated. No system prompts are published.
meta.3: Meta lists by kind the guardrails around one of its own products, the Muse agent launched on 8 September 2026: a separate agent, Sentinel, that alone approves actions through connectors and all traffic leaving over the network, classifiers against prompt injection and for the browser, filters on email, and human approval for payments. These are security controls. For Meta AI, the Muse Spark report names the kinds of safeguard around the model, integrity checks, guardrails, production system prompts and classifiers watching for cyber misuse, without listing them, and says only that "An external human red team identified a handful of valid jailbreaks; the majority of these were subsequently patched in Meta AI prior to launch." A red team is a group brought in to attack a system; a jailbreak is a way of getting a model past its rules. For developers, Llama Guard 4, Prompt Guard 2 and CyberSecEval are published tools, and Llama Guard 4 lists fourteen hazard categories. Some changes to the safeguards on its products are announced in its newsroom, mostly for teenagers: the pause of teenagers' access to AI characters in January 2026, added as an update to a post of October 2025, and in July 2026 an AI system that flags signs of distress in teenagers' conversations for review before parents are alerted. Nothing holds these changes in one register.
meta.4: No set of hard constraints, no consultation, and no body with authority over either. Meta's scaling framework names the propensities a model spec will describe, among them honesty, refusal and acquiescence to shutdown, and its Muse Spark report refers to an internal behaviour specification. Neither document is published, and neither names a rule the model may never break. A member of Meta's Oversight Board, Krishnaswamy, said in March 2026: "We don't have a mandate on gen-AI, but it's something we're trying to understand." Every change to its rules on behaviour in the period was announced as public relations, under pressure from outside: the removal of romantic role-play with minors in August 2025, through a spokesperson's statement to Reuters, and the worldwide pause of teenagers' access to AI characters in January 2026, through an update added to an old blog post and an exclusive given to TechCrunch.
meta.practices_published: It publishes no constitution, so there is no text to put under a licence.
meta.practices_engaged: Results of tests against the internal constitution are published, though the constitution is not (1). Outside evaluators are involved and named, Apollo Research, which tested Muse Spark independently, an external red team, and biosecurity consultants including SecureBio, though on terms that are not stated (1). The report also credits SecureBio, the Center for AI Safety and Charlemagne Labs with benchmarks that Meta ran itself. Meta names who confirms changes to its risk framework, the Director of Alignment and Risk and the Chief AI Officer, and no one for a document about how its models behave (0).

xai.1: No constitution. What xAI has published about how its models should behave is in system prompts: a safety prompt for its API models that lists twelve disallowed activities and ranks itself above every other instruction, and a short policy block for Grok 4.1, all for models retired in May 2026. The acceptable use policy governs users and says nothing about the model ("You are free to use our Service so long as you use it to be a good human, act safely and responsibly, comply with the law, not harm people, and respect our guardrails"). The Frontier AI Framework covers systemic risks, and on everyday behaviour it says only that models are trained to decline requests showing clear intent to engage in criminal or dual-use activity, and trained against deception and sycophancy. Deployments for governments are marketed on "direct, unfiltered answers", with no statement about behaviour attached. The framework acknowledges that they may differ: "the full functionality of our models may be available to only a limited set of trusted parties, partners, and government agencies". A post of December 2025 announces "government-optimized foundation models to support classified operational workloads", and neither says what rules apply to them.
xai.2: xai-org/grok-prompts published the system prompts of xAI's products from May to November 2025. Each change can be read line by line in its commit history, and almost none is explained: thirteen of the fourteen commits carry the note "Updated grok prompts" and no reason. One change bundles an edit to the repository's description, a deleted file, code that inserts stored memories into conversations, and three new safety prompts. The repository stopped at Grok 4.1. Every model it covers was retired from the API in May 2026, and the prompts of Grok 4.3, 4.5 and 4.6, and of Grok 4.7 since 21 September 2026, are unpublished, although xAI said in May 2025: "The public will be able to review them and give feedback to every prompt change that we make to Grok." The Frontier AI Framework has four versions, none numbered and none linked from the others, and its revision of 30 June 2026 dropped the two numerical criteria for deployment that the December 2025 version set, with no record of the change.
xai.3: The framework names three kinds of safeguard (safety training, system prompts and filters). The model cards describe layers of refusal, with reported rates, and name the filters by harm class: child sexual abuse material, self-harm, biological and chemical weapons, and for current models safeguards specific to cyber attacks as well. The Grok 4 card also names the products they run on, and for current models the cards say only that filters run "on some deployment surfaces". There is no inventory across products and no process for changing them. The restrictions on image editing of January 2026 were announced in a post by X's Safety account (X has belonged to xAI since 2025), and are recorded in no xAI framework, model card or register.
xai.4: A named set of disallowed activities, marked as overriding every other instruction, was published for models retired in May 2026, and nothing like it is published for current models. There is no mechanism for comment and no commitment. The framework reserves the right to change course alone: "We may change our approach over time as we gain further experience and insights on the projected capabilities of future frontier models."
xai.practices_published: It publishes no constitution. The system prompts it has published carry open licences, the GNU Affero General Public License 3.0 for grok-prompts and Apache 2.0 for Grok Build (1).
xai.practices_engaged: Every Grok model card reports how often the model complies with requests its refusal policy says to refuse, by policy category, against a policy published only for models since retired (1). A testing agreement with CAISI, the United States' Center for AI Standards and Innovation, signed in May 2026, has produced no published evaluation of any Grok model (1). The model cards describe training against the refusal policy, and xAI explained two Grok incidents in 2025 and none since.

moonshot.1:
No constitution. The closest published statement of how its models should behave is the default system prompt in the quickstart guide for its API, which reads "You are Kimi, an AI assistant provided by Moonshot AI... You provide users with safe, helpful, and accurate answers. You also refuse to answer any questions involving terrorism, racism, pornography, violence, or similar harmful content." It is sample code that a developer can leave out, and it commits Moonshot to nothing about its own deployments, so it scores 1. Nothing is said about coverage, with no statement for the Kimi app, the API, Kimi Business or the downloadable models, and the one clause of the K3 licence that bears on conduct governs the licensee's use, which "must comply with applicable laws and regulations".

The direction of travel is the notable part. The technical report for Kimi K2 (July 2025) had a real safety section. It described safety training from a set of examples chosen by people, across violence, fraud and discrimination, and a safety evaluation (its section 4.3) comparing how often attempts to push the model past its rules succeeded, against other models. The report for K2.5 (February 2026) has no section on safety at all. The report for K3 (July 2026) has one, section 6.2.2, which measures offensive cyber capability, the tier it calls most relevant to misuse risk, and cites the UK AISI and CAISI assessment; it says nothing about safety training or safeguards. Concordia AI's survey of 14 July 2026, published before K3, counts K2.5 among flagship releases that came "with no safety evaluation results at all".
moonshot.2: One narrow point in its favour: the Chinese user agreement carries both a date of update (24 August 2026) and a separate date of effect (31 August 2026), which gives seven days' notice, and the consumer terms carry a version number (v2). There is no archive and no record of what changed. An earlier, undated version of the consumer terms is still served at its own address, and nothing links to it. The platform's change log covers features, model launches, retirements and pricing; its one entry about policy says the terms "have been updated" without saying what changed. No system prompt used in production is published: the default prompt in the quickstart guide is sample code, and the chat template for K3, the format in which a conversation is handed to the model, holds no default prompt. Nothing says which policy governs which model.
moonshot.3: The filter on its API is described: it runs on input and output, names illegal, violent and pornographic content among what it catches, returns a content_filter error, and can be contested with the request_id when it fires in error. On the consumer app, the user agreement describes extra output filtering in minors' mode, and an earlier version of the terms says generated content passes automatic filtering. The platform terms ban "using variants, garbled characters, characters, homophones or other means to evade service detection". There is no inventory of guardrails by kind and no record of changes to them. The labelling of AI-generated content is disclosed, and is required by the labelling rules of the Cyberspace Administration of China: visible and hidden labels are applied by default, visible labels may be removed through a function Moonshot AI provides or on an approved application, and hidden labels may not be removed. None of the roughly forty repositories Moonshot AI publishes on GitHub is safety tooling.
moonshot.4: No named set of hard constraints, no consultation, and no channel for comment. Changes are made by the company alone, and continuing to use the service counts as accepting them.
moonshot.practices_published: It publishes no constitution, so there is no text to put under a licence.
moonshot.practices_engaged: The K2 report of July 2025 published a red-team of Kimi K2, run with Promptfoo across generic categories of harm and tied to no behaviour document, and it was not repeated for K2.5 or K3 (0). The UK AI Security Institute and the US Center for AI Standards and Innovation published a joint preliminary assessment of Kimi K3 on 23 July 2026, finding that "Kimi K3's safeguards did not prevent it from attempting cyber exploit development". The K3 report cites that assessment in its cyber section as reaching conclusions consistent with its own, and does not say Moonshot AI gave access; its section on third-party evaluation lists only Artificial Analysis, Vals AI and Arena (0). An independent academic safety evaluation of K2.5 (arXiv 2604.03121, April 2026) was carried out on the downloadable model without Moonshot's involvement.

aside.title: No filing number found
aside.text: Moonshot AI does not publish, anywhere we could find, its filing number with the Cyberspace Administration of China for its algorithms or its generative AI service: only its website licence (ICP) and its public security (公安网安) registrations. It almost certainly holds one, since it could not operate in China otherwise.

deepseek.1: No constitution. Apart from its R1 paper (2025), which says its safety training labelled answers against predefined safety guidelines, the only document of its own that says anything about how its models should behave is a disclosure page on how its algorithms work, of the kind the regulator requires: 《模型原理与训练方法说明》, an explanation of the model's principles and training methods. Its entire contribution is one sentence: in the optimisation stage DeepSeek builds "dedicated safety data to align the model, teaching it to give replies that conform to human values". No order of authority, no list of what the model refuses, no worked examples, and no rules for conflicts. The terms of use govern users, and the English and Chinese versions carry different dates (27 March 2026 and 5 September 2025) and different lists of prohibited content, with no change log to reconcile them. The model cards for V4-Pro and V4.1-Flash have no section on safety, limitations or responsible use.
deepseek.2: Nothing to score. The disclosure page has no date and no version. The API change log covers models and pricing. The terms keep no archive and point readers to the latest version: a new version "replaces the original terms" as soon as it is announced, and users are told to check the website themselves. DeepSeek published the web and app system prompts of V3-0324 and R1-0528 in their 2025 model cards, prompts that set only the assistant's identity and the date, and the R1 README says the app then used no system prompt, only templates for file upload and web search. Nothing of the kind has been published since V3.1 (August 2025), and nothing says which policy governs which model.
deepseek.3: A layer of moderation is reserved as a right in its contract, and the Chinese text claims more than the English: DeepSeek reserves the right to review "inputs and outputs", to set up "risk filtering mechanisms" and to build "feature databases of illegal content". The paper on its R1 model published in Nature (September 2025) says the model's own safety is "moderate", but "when coupled with the risk control system, the safety level of the model is increased to a superior standard". The paper's appendix describes that system as deployed on DeepSeek's official services: each user query is matched against a keyword list, and a flagged conversation is reviewed by DeepSeek-V3 against a prompt the paper publishes, which decides whether the answer is retracted. It was written for R1, and nothing has been published on the system since. The system is not in the downloadable model. Nothing on logging changes to guardrails.
deepseek.4: No named set of hard constraints on the model, no channel for comment, and no period of notice. Changes are made by the company alone and take effect as soon as they are published.
deepseek.practices_published: It publishes no constitution, so there is no text to put under a licence.
deepseek.practices_engaged: The R1 paper in Nature contained a real safety evaluation, with its method, but it concerns a model DeepSeek stopped serving on 21 August 2025, when its API and app moved to DeepSeek-V3.1, and it measures the model against benchmarks, one of them built on DeepSeek's own taxonomy of risks, with no constitution involved (1). We found no safety evaluation published for V3.1, V3.2, V4 or V4.1. The US Center for AI Standards and Innovation evaluated DeepSeek models in September 2025 on weights it downloaded, without the developer's involvement, and its follow-up assessment of V4 Pro in May 2026 covers capabilities only, so the most recent authoritative safety data concerns models no longer offered. No framework for frontier risks, no programme giving outsiders access, and no published process for approving changes.

aside.title: Behaviour that travels with the model
aside.text: Two things are worth knowing. First, the censorship also sits in the model itself. The US Center for AI Standards and Innovation found that "CCP censorship is built directly into DeepSeek models", testing copies downloaded from Hugging Face without touching DeepSeek's own service, so behaviour the company has never described travels with the model. Second, DeepSeek publishes its filing numbers with the Cyberspace Administration of China in full, with links to the regulator's notices.

page.title: How constitutions are governed
page.intro: Some AI companies publish a constitution, a document setting out how their models should[*](/about#why) behave. This view scores nine companies, as of September 2026, on two things: how transparent they are about the constitutions they publish, and the extent to which those constitutions are actually made to bind the models. The final score is the average of the two, and it ranks the companies.

sections.title: Motivation
blocks:
A constitution is the only public statement of how a company intends its models to behave, which makes it the reference against which any claim about a model’s behaviour can be checked. It can serve that purpose only if outsiders can see which models it governs and when it changes.

As of September 2026 significant changes can happen out of sight: a model deployed under rules nobody has published, a guardrail tightened or loosened without notice, a rule weakened before anything is said. This board scores what each company makes visible. It asks for disclosure, and says nothing about how a company should decide what its rules are.

sections.title: Detailed scoring
blocks:
### Where the rows come from

The board has two sources and no others. The four questions are the four asks of Polaris Collective's working paper "Model spec governance and transparency", in its draft of 10 September 2026. The ten best practices beside them come from "Emerging International Best Practices for AI Model Specs", a working paper by Edward Kembery and colleagues that is under review. Every row on the board carries the number of the note that names its source, and the paper's own words sit in the popover the row's name opens. Neither paper splits a question into checks, weighs one row against another, or says what earns a score. We did all three, and every score on the board is ours.

### How a figure is worked out

A question is split into checks, each scored from 0 to 4: three for each of the first two questions and two for the others. Every check carries a written description of what earns 0, what earns 2 and what earns 4, in the tables below. A question's own figure is the average of its checks. A best practice is scored 0, 1 or 2. Four of them carry a description of each score of their own, and the others share one scale.

The board shows every score out of 10, as its share of the scale it was given on: a check scored 3 of 4 shows 7.5, and a practice scored 1 of 2 shows 5.0. The score as given is in the panel that opens on it.

Each row belongs to one figure and one only, and every row of a figure counts the same. What is published has eleven rows, the ten checks and the licence practice, so each counts for 1/11 of it and a question with three checks counts for 3/11. What it engages has eight, all of them practices, each counting for 1/8. Every row says under its name how much it counts for.

**The final score averages the two figures**, each counting for half, and companies are ranked on it. Companies level on it share a place. The two figures measure different things, what a company has published and what it says about its own practice, so both stay on the board under the final score and a reader can see which half a company earned it on.

Below, every question, check and practice is named as it is on the board. The tables say what earns 0, 2 and 4 on each check, and a score of 1 or 3 falls between the descriptions either side of it.

### Rules we added to the descriptions*

Some cases fit none of the descriptions above, or two of them. We decided each once, for all nine companies.

- A sentence naming a class of models that includes the most-used ones counts as a statement of coverage, and is worth 4 of 4 on coverage stated (1.2).
- System prompts a company publishes count as a partial constitution, worth 2 of 4 on constitution published (1.1), and a history that shows each change to them line by line, without reasons, is worth 2 of 4 on changes explained (2.2).
- On versions kept (2.1) a bare date is worth 0, and a version label, a versions menu, an earlier text still online or a published promise to keep past versions is worth 1.
- Coverage that a document implies without stating it is worth 2 of 4 on coverage stated (1.2), as the description of a 2 says.
- A published safety evaluation against the company's own policies, with its results, is worth 1 of 2 on adherence tests published (S2).
- One disclosure earns points on one row only, the row it fits best.
- Guardrails listed by category for one platform are worth 3 of 4 on guardrails disclosed (3.1).
- Guardrail changes a company announces on its own channels, with no register, are worth 2 of 4 on guardrail changes logged (3.2), as the description of a 2 says.
- A special regime a company acknowledges without describing it is worth 2 of 4 on special deployments (1.3), as the description of a 2 says.

*These rules are our own choices, made on 26 September 2026 so that every company is scored the same way where the descriptions left a case open. They come from neither working paper.

### The best practices, figure by figure

The ten best practices come from the second working paper named above, note 6 under the board. Each is named below as it is on the board, followed by what the paper asks and where it asks it.

One practice is counted in what is published, because it is a fact about the published text.
Four are counted in what it engages and can be checked by anyone from public sources.

Four more are counted in the same figure, and nobody outside a company can see whether it follows them. The paper asks companies to say so publicly, so each is scored 0, 1 or 2 on what the company publishes, and 0 when it publishes nothing.
One is scored for nobody, for the reason note 7 gives, and is counted in neither figure.

The paper gives no description of what 0, 1 and 2 mean on a practice. In our scoring, 2 is the practice in full, 1 part of it or a weaker form of it, and 0 means we found nothing published.

### How we looked

Every score was first given by hand, by reading documents. No model judged any row in that reading, and no score was taken from another ranking. The reading was done between 18 and 21 September 2026, and the sources it rests on are listed company by company below.

For each company we searched its own pages first: the constitution or policy document where one exists, the developer documentation, the model cards and system cards, the terms of service and usage policy, the change logs and release notes, and the safety or frontier framework. We then searched for the company by name against the practices it had not answered, and read the outside sources listed below, among them the EU Code of Practice signatory list, the Stanford Foundation Model Transparency Index, and the evaluations published by the UK AI Security Institute and the US Center for AI Standards and Innovation. For the four practices only a company can show, the search was run one practice at a time across all nine companies, so that each practice was judged the same way everywhere.

Every row was read again on 23 and 24 September 2026, and the passage behind each score was recorded with its address and its date.

On 25 September 2026 an audit carried out with language models checked every row against its sources and found documents that reading had missed. Where a second model confirmed a correction, the score was changed to follow the board's descriptions of each score, and the rows it changed cite the documents it found with that date. Corrections that turned on a rule the board had not written down were held, and so were corrections that would raise Anthropic, since the models that carried out the audit are Anthropic's. A person decided both on 26 September 2026: the nine rules listed above were written down and applied to every company, and four corrections raising Anthropic were approved. The rows they changed cite the audit's sources with that date.

**Where nothing is published, the board says nothing is published.** A 0 is not a judgement that a company does not do something. It says we looked and found nothing public, and a company may well follow a practice without saying so. Every row on the board rests on a passage quoted with its address in the popover behind the score, or on a sentence there saying where we looked and found nothing. Two searches failed outright, and both are named under Limitations: the Chinese regulatory filings, and older copies of pages that carry no date.

Tell us if we are wrong. The button at the bottom right of this page sends us a note, and a correction that carries the address of the document is the most useful thing anyone can send.

### How to read the scores

**Publishing a constitution and covering models with it are scored separately.** Alibaba's constitution names no model, and on a single "has a constitution" column it would score the same as one that binds a company's products.

**The rows say more than the figure.** OpenAI and Anthropic are the two highest on what is published and fall short in opposite ways. OpenAI keeps every version at a dated address, where Anthropic's one earlier version survives at its old address and nothing records the edits since. Anthropic names the things its models must never do as a closed set, where OpenAI's top level points at detailed policies it does not publish.

**The two figures do not agree with each other.** Meta publishes little and is fourth on what it engages, level with xAI, which leaves it sixth on the final score. Mistral AI is fourth on what is published and scores 0 on what it engages, the only company that does, which leaves it seventh. That is why both figures stay on the board under the final score.

**Six of the nine companies publish no constitution**, and what they publish instead decides their first figure. xAI and Mistral AI publish system prompts, which we count as a partial constitution, and they are third and fourth on what is published, ahead of Alibaba, whose full constitution names no model and keeps no change log. Google DeepMind publishes guidelines for its app and is sixth. Meta, Moonshot AI and DeepSeek publish fragments and hold the three lowest places. Among the three that publish a constitution, the change log is what separates them.

### Who the companies are

Some trading names mislead, so here are the companies behind three of them. Moonshot AI is Beijing Moonshot AI Technology (北京月之暗面科技有限公司), which makes the Kimi models. DeepSeek is 杭州深度求索人工智能基础技术研究有限公司, of Hangzhou, spun out of the High-Flyer (幻方) quantitative investment fund. Mistral AI is Mistral AI SAS, of Paris.

sections.title: Limitations
blocks:
Both working papers were written to argue for change, and scoring them gives them more precision than they were designed for. The descriptions of each score are ours, and so are the nine rules we added on 26 September 2026 where they left a case open. A different reading could move a company by a few points. The wider picture would stay: all nine fall short on the change log, none offers a comment window before one of the things a model must never do is weakened, and none covers government, defence and other special deployments.

Every score rests on a document found and dated, in the reading of 18 to 21 September 2026, in the audit of 25 September 2026, or when its findings were applied on 26 September 2026. These points are open.

- **Alibaba's constitution serves no text at its own address.** A plain request to it returns an application shell and no document, so the text used is the copy this index holds, 210 passages of it, word for word, at [its April 2026 version](/doc-reader/?spec=alibaba--model-spec@2026-04-00). The index keeps only passages that bear on a behaviour, so prefaces and boilerplate are not in it. The preface's invitation to public comment and the overview's acknowledgement of safeguards the service applies around the model are both confirmed, and there is no statement of coverage anywhere in the document. Anyone who tries to check a quotation at that address will meet the same shell.
- **Alibaba's list of guardrail categories for Model Studio was last updated on 23 September 2026**, after our reading, and no earlier copy was checked. Its 3 on guardrails disclosed rests on that page.
- **No older copies of the undated pages were found.** Where a page carries no date and no earlier copy, a quiet edit to it would not show. This matters most for Google, where three of the relevant documents carry no date at all, and for DeepSeek, whose disclosure page has no earlier copy anyone could find.
- **The Chinese regulatory filings were not found.** The Cyberspace Administration of China publishes its lists as attachments that could not be retrieved. So when this board says Moonshot AI publishes no filing number, it means none appears on Moonshot AI's own sites.
- **Whether Anthropic has signed the EU Code of Practice is unconfirmed.** Its July 2025 post says it "intends to sign"; its own page of voluntary commitments does not list it. No score depends on this.
- **Which chapters of the EU Code of Practice Mistral has signed is unconfirmed.** The European Commission's list names Mistral with no exception, and sets out chapters only for xAI. No score depends on this.
- **Which Anthropic models do not fully fit its constitution** is not written down: the constitution names none, and the point about military models comes from a spokesperson quoted by TIME. Coverage of Claude Mythos's system card says it was trained with the constitution, so it is not counted among them.
- **What Meta's log of updates to its Community Standards contains could not be established**, so the reading that it does not cover AI is an inference nobody has checked.
- **The release date of Kimi K3 is disputed** between Moonshot AI's own blog (27 July 2026, for the downloadable model) and the UK AI Security Institute and Wikipedia (16 July 2026). No score depends on this.
- **All scores are ours.** None comes from an established, published scoring method.

sections.title: What comes next
blocks:
The scores will be revisited as companies publish, and a correction that carries the address of a document is the most useful thing a reader can send. The four questions come from a working paper that is still being written, so they may change with it.

The next view, how constitutions are regulated, follows the same documents into law: which jurisdictions require a constitution to be described, to whom, and whether any requires it to be published or its changes to be recorded.
