open_questions.title: Anthropic and Meta both score nought on who approves a change, and each names who approves changes to a risk framework
open_questions.question: Anthropic's Responsible Scaling Policy names a proposer, the CEO and the RSO, and an approver, the Board in consultation with the LTBT, for changes to that policy. Section 5.1 of Meta's Advanced AI Scaling Framework says an update is confirmed by its Director of Alignment and Risk and its Chief AI Officer. Neither publishes an approval arrangement for a constitution, which is what the row asks about, so both are nought as the row is written.
open_questions.what_would_settle_it: Deciding whether the row scores a published approval arrangement for any governing document or only for a constitution, saying which in the row's own words, and applying it to all nine companies at once.

open_questions.title: The two figures are added, and the condition set for adding them was never met
open_questions.question: Adding what is published to what it engages was argued on the ground that the practices would be anchored as the checks are. No full description of 0, 1 and 2 was written for S1 to S5; the rules of 26 September 2026 say what earns a 1 in two cases, an open licence on a partial text and a safety evaluation against the company's own policies. Fourteen of the thirty-two non-zero cells of what it engages sit on S2 to S5, and they decide places: OpenAI leads Anthropic by less than what one point on any of them is worth, and DeepSeek is eighth, ahead of Moonshot AI, on the strength of its 1 on published adherence tests.
open_questions.what_would_settle_it: Writing an anchor for each of S1 to S5, then rescoring those cells against it.

open_questions.title: OpenAI leads Anthropic by one point on one check
open_questions.question: OpenAI leads Anthropic by about 0.11 out of 10, 6.34 against 6.22, which is exactly what one point on one check is worth. The two are level on what they engage, 5.6 each, and their rows on what is published differ by a single point, net. Both moved on 26 September 2026: the rule on coverage stated as a class raised OpenAI by one point, and the four corrections approved for Anthropic raised it by three points on checks and one on a practice. Without that rule the two would be level. The audit that proposed the Anthropic corrections was carried out with Anthropic's models, and a person approved them. Any single point read the other way on either company would tie them or reverse the order.
open_questions.what_would_settle_it: Saying on the board, where the order is shown, that the first two places are one check apart, and treating any further reading of either company's rows as a question for both at once.

open_questions.title: The sentence saying what a nought means is no longer in the table
open_questions.question: A nought records that nothing published was found, not that a company does not do the thing. That sentence is now behind a press or inside a section that opens shut, while sentences elsewhere read the figure as what a company does.
open_questions.what_would_settle_it: Putting it back where a reader meets the noughts.

open_questions.title: Coverage stated as a class counts as stated
open_questions.question: We score a sentence that names a class of models, such as the models that power a company's products, as a full statement of coverage when the most-used models belong to it. OpenAI's coverage stated rose from 3 to 4, level with Anthropic, whose constitution names no model either. The other choice was 3 for both, keeping 4 for a document that lists its models: each of the two leaders would lose 0.11 on the final score and their order would stand. The rule makes naming models unnecessary. A reader cannot tell from the document alone whether a given model is covered, only from what the company says elsewhere, such as a system card saying a model was trained on it. It rewards the broad sentence both leaders already wrote, and gives no company a reason to publish a list of models.
open_questions.what_would_settle_it: Deciding whether the memo's ask, that no deployed model goes ungoverned, can be checked without a list of models, and if it cannot, scoring 3 on coverage stated for every company that names a class and no model.

open_questions.title: Published system prompts count as a partial constitution
open_questions.question: We count the system prompts a company publishes as a partial constitution. xAI already scored 2 on constitution published on that basis. The rule moved Mistral AI from 0 to 2 there, from 1 to 2 on hard constraints listed and from 0 to 1 on the open licence, and moved Mistral AI and xAI each from 0 to 2 on changes explained, because the prompts' history on GitHub shows every change line by line. Mistral AI rose from 0.9 to 1.7 on the final score, and to fourth on what is published, ahead of Alibaba, which publishes a full constitution. Read the other way, as a layer of their own that is no constitution, Mistral AI would be eighth, below DeepSeek, and xAI, losing its earlier points on the same basis, fourth below Google DeepMind. The rule rewards publishing the prompts of one product as if they were a behaviour document. Mistral AI's govern one coding agent, a user can replace them, and what they mark as not overridable is a list of confirmations that a flag switches off. xAI's govern models retired in May 2026. Moonshot AI stays at 1 for a sample prompt in its quickstart, which governs no product, and the prompts DeepSeek published for two 2025 models set only the assistant's identity and the date, so they add nothing. The constitutions board, which scores the documents themselves, still counts neither xAI nor Mistral AI as publishing a constitution, so the two boards read the same texts differently. Mistral AI stays at 1 on versions kept, although the same history keeps every earlier prompt at a permanent address, which is part of what earns xAI 2 there.
open_questions.what_would_settle_it: Deciding whether the board scores the rules a company publishes for its models in whatever form, or only a document meant to govern its models in general, then reading system prompts the same way on both boards and on versions kept.

open_questions.title: A bare date is not a version
open_questions.question: On versions kept we score a date alone at 0, and a version label, a versions menu, an earlier text still online or a published promise to keep past versions at 1. No score moved. Alibaba and DeepSeek stay at 0 for a dated text with nothing else, Moonshot AI stays at 1 because an earlier version of its terms is still served at ?version=v1, and Mistral AI stays at 1 for a versions menu on its usage policy that lists nothing. The other choice, 1 for any dated text, would have raised Alibaba and DeepSeek by 0.11 each on the final score and moved no place. The line is thin. An empty versions menu earns what a dated text does not, which rewards the fixture over the archive, and a promise to keep past versions earns as much as keeping one.
open_questions.what_would_settle_it: Writing into the check's description which of these earns a 1, and deciding whether a versions menu that lists nothing should.

open_questions.title: Implied coverage earns 2, except where there is almost nothing to cover
open_questions.question: We score coverage a document implies without stating it at 2 on coverage stated, as the description of a 2 says. Alibaba rose from 0 to 2: its overview says Alibaba is training its models towards the Spec and speaks of the gap between its current production models and it. The sentence reports progress in training and states no scope. DeepSeek stays at 0, although its disclosure page describes every model it serves online, because the only behaviour it states is one sentence on safety training, too thin for coverage to mean anything. That exception is a judgement the descriptions do not contain: read literally, DeepSeek's page would earn 2 as well, adding 0.23 to its final score and moving no place. Alibaba's 2 is worth 0.23 on its final score and did not move its place either. The rule scores the same kind of implication differently in a thin text and in a full one.
open_questions.what_would_settle_it: Deciding whether coverage stated can score anything where constitution published is at 1 or below, and writing that into the check's description.

open_questions.title: A safety evaluation against a company's own policies earns 1 on adherence tests
open_questions.question: We score a published safety evaluation against the company's own policies, with its results, at 1 of 2 on adherence tests published, as Google DeepMind and xAI were scored on 25 September 2026. DeepSeek rose from 0 to 1 for the safety report on R1, whose results stop at a model it stopped serving in August 2025. That point is what puts DeepSeek eighth, ahead of Moonshot AI: without it DeepSeek would score 0.65 and be last. The other choice, reading the practice as a test against a constitution only, would take Google DeepMind, xAI and DeepSeek back to 0 and move one place, DeepSeek's. The rule gives a benchmark of harmful requests the same point as a test of whether a model follows a written rule, and a single report on a model since withdrawn earns what a report on current models earns.
open_questions.what_would_settle_it: Writing a description of 0, 1 and 2 for this practice that says whether a test must be against the constitution or may be against any written policy of the company's, and whether results for withdrawn models count.

open_questions.title: One disclosure is counted once
open_questions.question: We count a disclosure on the one row it fits best. DeepSeek's R1 paper describes a filter that screens conversations on its own service. It earns DeepSeek 2 on guardrails disclosed, and it is not counted again as monitoring in use, where DeepSeek stays at 0. The other choice would have given DeepSeek 1 on monitoring in use, worth 0.31 on the final score, which would not have moved its place. The rule keeps one document from lifting a company on several rows at once, and it leaves open which row is the right one: a filter that retracts answers as they are given is a guardrail by the board's definition, and it is also the only thing DeepSeek has said about watching its models in use. Meta's 1 on monitoring in use rests on a sentence about automated monitoring after launch, which the rule does not touch.
open_questions.what_would_settle_it: Writing into the description of monitoring in use whether a filter that acts on each answer counts as monitoring, and checking every company's 1 there against it.

open_questions.title: Guardrails listed by category for one platform earn 3
open_questions.question: We score guardrails disclosed by category for one platform at 3 of 4, the precedent set for Mistral AI. Alibaba rose from 2 to 3 for Model Studio, its own model platform, which says its models carry compliance checks of their own and lists the categories of an optional guardrail. Meta rose from 1 to 3 for the guardrails of its Muse agent, listed by kind, the kinds of safeguard its Muse Spark report names for Meta AI, and the categories of Llama Guard. Seven of the nine companies now score 3 on this check and none scores 4, so the check separates almost nobody. The descriptions give 2 to a disclosure for one product, and 3 sits between that and an inventory across every product; the rule puts a single platform there whatever share of the company's products it is. The other choice, 2 for one platform, would have cost Meta and Alibaba 0.11 each on the final score, and any other company whose 3 rests on one platform the same, without moving a place. Alibaba's page of categories was last updated on 23 September 2026, after our reading, and Meta's Muse guardrails are security controls, against prompt injection, leaks of personal data and unapproved payments.
open_questions.what_would_settle_it: Writing a description of a 3 on this check, and deciding whether a platform for developers and a single consumer product count the same.

open_questions.title: Changes announced on a company's own channels, with no register, earn 2
open_questions.question: We score guardrail changes a company announces on its own channels, with no register, at 2 of 4 on guardrail changes logged, as the description of a 2 says. Meta rose from 0 to 2 for posts in its newsroom: the pause of teenagers' access to AI characters, added in January 2026 as an update to a post of October 2025, and a system of July 2026 that flags signs of distress in teenagers' conversations. xAI rose from 1 to 2 for the restriction on image editing that X's Safety account announced in January 2026; X has belonged to xAI since 2025. Six of the nine now score 2 on this check and none more. The rule rewards a blog post, or a post on a social network made under pressure from regulators, as much as anything short of a register, and it asks nothing about how many changes are announced: one announced change among many silent ones earns the same 2. The other choice, 1 wherever changes are announced case by case, would have lowered six companies by 0.11 each on the final score and moved no place.
open_questions.what_would_settle_it: Deciding whether a 2 needs most changes to be announced or any, and writing that into the check's description.

open_questions.title: A special regime acknowledged but not described earns 2
open_questions.question: We score a special regime a company acknowledges without describing it at 2 of 4 on special deployments, as the description of a 2 says. xAI rose from 0 to 2: section 2.3 of its Frontier AI Framework says that "the full functionality of our models may be available to only a limited set of trusted parties, partners, and government agencies", and its post of December 2025 announces government-optimised models for classified work. Google DeepMind stays at 0. It confirmed an agreement letting the Pentagon use Gemini on classified networks and has not acknowledged that the rules there differ; that they differ was reported by the press, citing The Information. The rule gives a sentence about tiered access in a risk framework the same 2 as Anthropic's statement, in its constitution, that some of its models do not fully fit it, and it turns on what a company admits: a company that says nothing scores 0 whatever it deploys. xAI's third place rests on three of these rules together. Its 2 here, or its 2 on changes explained, would each have lifted it above Google DeepMind alone, and its 2 on guardrail changes logged would not.
open_questions.what_would_settle_it: Deciding whether acknowledging a deployment is enough, or whether the company must say that the rules there differ, and writing that into the check's description of a 2.

openai.published: The Model Spec sits at a dated address with every past version, under an open licence, and says what it covers. It names kinds of deployment without saying whether government use is among those it governs, and its change log explains changes only in part.
openai.engages: Just over half marks. It says how its public text relates to the one it trains on and that models are monitored in use, and it published one set of adherence tests that has not been kept current. Its outside evaluators test other risks, and no threshold decides whether a model is released.

anthropic.published: Its constitution is published under an open licence, says which models it covers and lists its hard constraints in full. Its change log is the gap: there is none, the 2023 version is still online with no link back to it, and nothing records later edits, though Anthropic has committed to publish a newer trained-on text within 90 days of deploying a model on it.
anthropic.engages: Just over half marks. It says it trains its models on the constitution, uses the same text inside and monitors models in use, and outside evaluators have tested its models for other risks. It publishes a claim of adherence with no method, and no threshold a model must pass before release.

alibaba.published: It publishes a constitution and names its hard constraints, though some are set by policy documents it does not publish, and it says the text is open source without naming a licence. It implies without stating that the document covers its production models, keeps no change log, and lists by category the guardrails of its own model platform.
alibaba.engages: Low. There is some sign that models are trained on the document, and it says the public text matches its internal behaviour standards, and its AAIG lab has published scores against the document for two Qwen models that stop before the current line. Nothing is published on monitoring.

google.published: No single constitution: its rules for the Gemini app are spread across several documents with different owners, and the model cards tie its safety policies to named models. It describes the guardrails it offers developers in detail and announces some changes to its guardrails, with no register.
google.engages: Its model cards publish adherence tests and a launch threshold for child safety against the safety policies they list, and it uses outside testers and describes some training and monitoring. Nothing is published on who approves a change to the rules.

mistral.published: No constitution. It publishes the system prompts of its coding agent under an open licence, with every change shown line by line and a short list of approvals marked as not overridable, and it describes its guardrails for developers with some record of how they change.
mistral.engages: Nothing found on any of the eight practices, from training on a document to testing or monitoring models against it.

meta.published: Little: no constitution and no list of hard constraints, a short record of versions of its framework, fragments of intended behaviour in a template prompt and rules for teenagers, and guardrails described for developers and listed by kind for its Muse agent, with some changes to them announced in its newsroom.
meta.engages: It publishes some adherence testing, uses outside testers and says its models are trained and monitored against internal policies, all without a published constitution. It has committed in writing to publish one, with tests against it.

xai.published: No constitution. A list of disallowed activities marked as overriding every other instruction was published for its 2025 API models, since retired, with a prompt log that shows each change line by line and stopped in November 2025. It gives a partial account of its guardrails, announces some changes to them on X, and says government agencies may get fuller functionality without saying what rules apply.
xai.engages: Low. Its model cards test how often Grok complies with requests its refusal policy says to refuse, it signed an outside testing agreement with no published result, and it describes training and monitoring against a refusal policy published only for models since retired.

moonshot.published: No constitution. The nearest thing is a default system prompt in its developer guide. It describes the content filter on its API and in its app, and little else is published about its rules or how they change.
moonshot.engages: Almost nothing: a description of some training against internal policies. Its one published safety test, a red-team of a model since withdrawn, is tied to no behaviour document.

deepseek.published: No constitution. Beyond the disclosure its regulator requires, its R1 paper of 2025 describes its safety training and its risk control system, and almost nothing else is published about its rules.
deepseek.engages: Little: a description of training against an internal policy, and a safety evaluation of R1, a model it no longer serves, against its own standards.
